sectionTitle: Chemical bonds, ionic, covalent and metallic

specStatements.text: There are three types of strong chemical bonds: ionic, covalent and metallic. For ionic bonding the particles are oppositely charged ions. For covalent bonding the particles are atoms which share pairs of electrons. For metallic bonding the particles are atoms which share delocalised electrons.
Ionic bonding occurs in compounds formed from metals combined with non-metals.
Covalent bonding occurs in most non-metallic elements and in compounds of non-metals.
Metallic bonding occurs in metallic elements and alloys.
Students should be able to explain chemical bonding in terms of electrostatic forces and the transfer or sharing of electrons.

When a metal atom reacts with a non-metal atom electrons in the outer shell of the metal atom are transferred. Metal atoms lose electrons to become positively charged ions. Non-metal atoms gain electrons to become negatively charged ions. The ions produced by metals in Groups 1 and 2 and by non-metals in Groups 6 and 7 have the electronic structure of a noble gas (Group 0).
The electron transfer during the formation of an ionic compound can be represented by a dot and cross diagram, eg for sodium chloride
Students should be able to draw dot and cross diagrams for ionic compounds formed by metals in Groups 1 and 2 with non-metals in Groups 6 and 7.
The charge on the ions produced by metals in Groups 1 and 2 and by non-metals in Groups 6 and 7 relates to the group number of the element in the periodic table.
Students should be able to work out the charge on the ions of metals and non-metals from the group number of the element, limited to the metals in Groups 1 and 2, and non-metals in Groups 6 and 7.

An ionic compound is a giant structure of ions. Ionic compounds are held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions. These forces act in all directions in the lattice and this is called ionic bonding.

Students should be able to:
deduce that a compound is ionic from a diagram of its structure in one of the specified forms
describe the limitations of using dot and cross, ball and stick, two and three-dimensional diagrams to represent a giant ionic structure
work out the empirical formula of an ionic compound from a given model or diagram that shows the ions in the structure.
Students should be familiar with the structure of sodium chloride but do not need to know the structures of other ionic compounds.
When atoms share pairs of electrons, they form covalent bonds. These bonds between atoms are strong.
Covalently bonded substances may consist of small molecules.
Students should be able to recognise common substances that consist of small molecules from their chemical formula.
Some covalently bonded substances have very large molecules, such as polymers.
Some covalently bonded substances have giant covalent structures, such as diamond and silicon dioxide.

Students should be able to:

represent the covalent bonds in small molecules, in the repeating units of polymers and in part of giant covalent structures, using a line to represent a single bond
describe the limitations of using dot and cross, ball and stick, two and three-dimensional diagrams to represent molecules or giant structures
deduce the molecular formula of a substance from a given model or diagram in these forms showing the atoms and bonds in the molecule.
Metals consist of giant structures of atoms arranged in a regular pattern.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should be familiar with the structure of sodium chloride but do not need to know the structures of other ionic compounds.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Sodium chloride is the only ionic structure taught here. Every description of a giant ionic lattice, and every question that asks a student to recall or reason about the arrangement of ions, uses sodium chloride. Other ionic compounds appear only where the specification independently allows them: as formulae or charges worked out from group number (4.2.1.2), as dot and cross diagrams of Group 1 and 2 metals with Group 6 and 7 non-metals (4.2.1.2), or as an empirical formula counted from a model that is supplied in the question (4.2.1.3). No structure of magnesium oxide, calcium fluoride or any other ionic compound is taught or assumed.

scopeNotes.statement: limited to the metals in Groups 1 and 2, and non-metals in Groups 6 and 7
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every ionic charge a student is asked to work out here comes from Group 1, 2, 6 or 7 - sodium, potassium, magnesium, calcium, oxygen, sulfur, chlorine, fluorine. Transition metal ions, Group 3 to 5 ions and polyatomic ions such as sulfate or nitrate are never used as items to be deduced, because the specification does not require the charge on those ions to be worked out from the periodic table.

scopeNotes.statement: for ionic compounds formed by metals in Groups 1 and 2 with non-metals in Groups 6 and 7
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Dot and cross work is confined to compounds of a Group 1 or Group 2 metal with a Group 6 or Group 7 non-metal - sodium chloride, magnesium chloride, magnesium oxide, potassium sulfide and the like. Students are never asked to draw the electron transfer for compounds outside that set.

scopeNotes.statement: the molecules of hydrogen, chlorine, oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen chloride, water, ammonia and methane
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Dot and cross diagrams for covalent molecules are taught and tested only for these eight molecules. Other molecules (for example carbon dioxide) are used only where a different skill applies - recognising a small molecule from its formula, or reading a molecular formula from a supplied model - never as a dot and cross diagram to be drawn from memory.

concepts.definition: There are three types of strong chemical bond: ionic, covalent and metallic. Each is a strong electrostatic attraction, but they differ in which particles are involved and in what happens to the outer electrons.
Bonding in which the particles are oppositely charged ions. It occurs in compounds formed from metals combined with non-metals, for example sodium chloride and magnesium oxide.

Bonding in which the particles are atoms which share pairs of electrons. It occurs in most non-metallic elements, such as oxygen and chlorine, and in compounds of non-metals, such as water and methane.
Bonding in which the particles are atoms which share delocalised electrons. It occurs in metallic elements and in alloys.

The force of attraction between opposite electric charges. All three types of strong bond are explained by electrostatic attraction: between oppositely charged ions in ionic bonding, between the shared pair of electrons and the two nuclei in covalent bonding, and between the metal atoms and the delocalised electrons they share in metallic bonding.
A charged particle formed when an atom loses or gains electrons. The charge arises because the number of electrons no longer equals the number of protons.
When a metal atom reacts with a non-metal atom, the electrons in the outer shell of the metal atom are transferred away. Metal atoms lose electrons to become positively charged ions.
Non-metal atoms gain the electrons transferred from the metal atoms and so become negatively charged ions.

The ions produced by metals in Groups 1 and 2 and by non-metals in Groups 6 and 7 have the electronic structure of a noble gas (Group 0). For example Na (2,8,1) forms Na+ with the structure 2,8, and Cl (2,8,7) forms Cl- with the structure 2,8,8.

A diagram that represents the electron transfer during the formation of an ionic compound, using dots for the electrons of one atom and crosses for the electrons of the other so the transfer can be followed. Each ion is drawn in square brackets with its charge written outside.

The charge on the ions produced by metals in Groups 1 and 2 and by non-metals in Groups 6 and 7 relates to the group number: Group 1 forms 1+ ions, Group 2 forms 2+ ions, Group 6 forms 2- ions and Group 7 forms 1- ions.

An ionic compound is a giant structure of ions. There is no fixed small unit and no molecule - the regular arrangement of oppositely charged ions, called a lattice, continues throughout the whole substance.
Ionic compounds are held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions. These forces act in all directions in the lattice, and this is called ionic bonding.

The structure of sodium chloride can be represented as a dot and cross diagram, as a ball and stick model, and as two-dimensional and three-dimensional diagrams of the lattice. A diagram showing a regular repeating arrangement of oppositely charged particles tells you the compound is ionic.

concepts.term: Empirical formula of an ionic compound
concepts.definition: The simplest whole number ratio of the ions in the structure. It is worked out from a given model or diagram by counting the ions of each type and reducing the count to its simplest ratio - so a model with 4 sodium ions and 4 chloride ions gives NaCl, not Na4Cl4.

concepts.term: Limitations of models of a giant ionic structure
concepts.definition: A dot and cross diagram shows where the electrons have come from but shows nothing about how the ions are arranged. A ball and stick model shows the arrangement but the sticks are not real and the ions are drawn much too far apart. A two-dimensional diagram cannot show that the lattice extends in three dimensions, and every diagram shows only a tiny part of a structure that is in reality enormous.

When atoms share pairs of electrons, they form covalent bonds. These bonds between atoms are strong. A single covalent bond is one shared pair; a double bond is two shared pairs and a triple bond is three.

A covalently bonded substance may consist of small molecules - a fixed, small number of atoms held together by covalent bonds, such as H2, Cl2, O2, N2, HCl, H2O, NH3, CH4 and CO2. Common small molecules can be recognised from their chemical formula.
Some covalently bonded substances have very large molecules, such as polymers. A polymer molecule is still a molecule - a very long chain built from a repeating unit - not a giant lattice.

Some covalently bonded substances have giant covalent structures, such as diamond and silicon dioxide. Every atom is joined to its neighbours by strong covalent bonds throughout the whole structure, so there are no separate molecules.

A diagram showing the outer electrons of the bonded atoms, with each shared pair drawn in the overlap between two atoms. Students should be able to draw these for hydrogen, chlorine, oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen chloride, water, ammonia and methane - for example O2 has two shared pairs between the atoms and N2 has three.

A polymer is represented by drawing its repeating unit inside brackets with the subscript n outside, where n is a large number. The n does not stand for a particular value - it shows that the unit inside the brackets is repeated a great many times along the chain.

The covalent bonds in small molecules, in the repeating units of polymers and in part of giant covalent structures can be represented using a line to represent a single bond. One line stands for one shared pair of electrons, so a double bond is drawn as two lines.

concepts.term: Limitations of models of molecules and giant structures
concepts.definition: A dot and cross diagram shows which atom each electron came from but not the shape of the molecule or the relative sizes of the atoms. A ball and stick model shows shape but exaggerates the space between atoms and shows bonds as solid sticks. Two-dimensional diagrams flatten a three-dimensional shape, and any diagram of a giant covalent structure can show only a small part of it.

The molecular formula is deduced from a model or diagram by counting the actual number of atoms of each element in the molecule, not the bonds between them, and not reducing the count to its simplest ratio. A model of ethane with 2 carbon and 6 hydrogen atoms is C2H6, not CH3.
Metals consist of giant structures of atoms arranged in a regular pattern. The pattern continues throughout the whole piece of metal, so a metal has no molecules.

The electrons in the outer shell of metal atoms are delocalised and so are free to move through the whole structure. They no longer belong to any one atom. The sharing of these delocalised electrons gives rise to strong metallic bonds.
A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements. Metallic bonding occurs in alloys as well as in metallic elements, so brass and steel are held together by metallic bonds.

misconceptions.question: Does any compound made from two different elements have ionic bonding?
misconceptions.correct: Ionic bonding occurs in compounds formed from metals combined with non-metals. A compound of two non-metals is covalently bonded.
misconceptions.misconception: If a compound is made of two different elements then the atoms must have swapped electrons, so it is ionic.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Ionic bonding is usually taught first and is often introduced simply as 'what happens when two elements combine'. Students remember the outcome - a compound - without holding on to the condition that one element must be a metal.
misconceptions.correction: Check the periodic table before deciding. Metal plus non-metal gives ionic bonding; non-metal plus non-metal gives covalent bonding. Water and carbon dioxide are compounds, but hydrogen, oxygen and carbon are all non-metals, so both are covalent.

misconceptions.question: Can an element have covalent bonding, or only a compound?
misconceptions.correct: Covalent bonding occurs in most non-metallic elements as well as in compounds of non-metals.
misconceptions.misconception: Bonding only happens when two different elements join, so a bottle of oxygen gas has no bonds in it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Bonding is introduced through reactions, where different elements combine. Students then attach the idea of bonding to 'compound' and think of an element as loose, unbonded atoms.
misconceptions.correction: Oxygen gas is O2 - two oxygen atoms sharing two pairs of electrons. Hydrogen, chlorine, nitrogen and oxygen are all non-metallic elements held together by covalent bonds.

misconceptions.question: What type of bonding is there in an alloy such as brass?
misconceptions.correct: Metallic bonding occurs in metallic elements and alloys, so brass has metallic bonding.
misconceptions.misconception: Brass contains two different elements, so it must be a compound with ionic or covalent bonding.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate 'two elements together' with compounds. An alloy looks like one substance, so it feels like a compound rather than a mixture.
misconceptions.correction: An alloy is a mixture of metals. Every atom in it is a metal atom, so all the outer electrons are delocalised and the bonding throughout is metallic.

misconceptions.question: Are electrons shared in ionic bonding?
misconceptions.correct: In ionic bonding electrons are transferred, not shared. Sharing pairs of electrons is covalent bonding; sharing delocalised electrons is metallic bonding.
misconceptions.misconception: Atoms share electrons in all types of bonding - ionic bonding is just sharing between a metal and a non-metal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'share' appears in two of the three definitions, and students blur transfer and sharing because both end with full outer shells.
misconceptions.correction: Match the word to the bond: ionic - transfer, giving oppositely charged ions; covalent - atoms share pairs of electrons; metallic - atoms share delocalised electrons. In sodium chloride the electron leaves sodium completely and stays on chlorine.

misconceptions.question: What actually holds the ions together in an ionic compound?
misconceptions.correct: Strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions hold them together.
misconceptions.misconception: The bond is the transfer of the electron - the electron jumping across is what sticks the two particles together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The electron transfer is the dramatic, memorable step in the story, so students identify it as the bond. The attraction that follows is invisible and easy to skip.
misconceptions.correction: Transfer is how the ions are made; the bond is what happens next. Once sodium is Na+ and chlorine is Cl-, the opposite charges attract electrostatically, and that attraction is the ionic bond.

misconceptions.question: Does a sodium atom lose one electron or gain seven?
misconceptions.correct: Metal atoms lose electrons to become positively charged ions, so sodium loses its one outer electron.
misconceptions.misconception: Sodium has one outer electron and needs eight, so it gains seven electrons to fill the shell.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn the rule 'atoms want a full outer shell' and apply it by filling the shell up, without asking which route involves moving fewer electrons or which element is the metal.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is explicit: electrons in the outer shell of the metal atom are transferred away. Losing one electron leaves sodium with 2,8 - the electronic structure of neon - which is a full outer shell too.

misconceptions.question: Why is an ion that has lost electrons positive?
misconceptions.correct: Losing negatively charged electrons leaves more protons than electrons, so the ion is positively charged.
misconceptions.misconception: Losing something makes you smaller, so losing electrons should make the charge negative and gaining them should make it positive.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Lose' and 'negative' both feel like decrease, and students reason about the change rather than about the balance of charges left behind.
misconceptions.correction: Count the charges. Sodium has 11 protons and 11 electrons; lose one electron and there are 11 positives to 10 negatives, so the ion is Na+. Chlorine gains one electron, so 17 protons to 18 electrons gives Cl-.

misconceptions.question: What is the charge on an ion of a Group 6 or Group 7 element?
misconceptions.correct: Group 6 non-metals form 2- ions and Group 7 non-metals form 1- ions.
misconceptions.misconception: The charge is always the group number, so a Group 6 ion is 6- and a Group 7 ion is 7-.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule works for Groups 1 and 2, where charge equals group number, so students over-generalise it to the right-hand side of the table.
misconceptions.correction: For metals the charge equals the group number because those electrons are lost. For non-metals count how many electrons are needed to fill the outer shell: Group 6 needs 2, giving 2-; Group 7 needs 1, giving 1-.

misconceptions.question: Does an ion have the same electronic structure as its atom?
misconceptions.correct: No. The ions produced by metals in Groups 1 and 2 and non-metals in Groups 6 and 7 have the electronic structure of a noble gas.
misconceptions.misconception: The element is still magnesium, so the electron arrangement written down for magnesium must still apply to the magnesium ion.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know the identity of the element is fixed by the protons, and wrongly extend 'nothing has changed' to the electrons, which are exactly what has changed.
misconceptions.correction: Adjust the electron count for the charge. Mg is 2,8,2; Mg2+ has lost two electrons and is 2,8 - the structure of neon. O is 2,6; O2- has gained two and is 2,8.

misconceptions.question: How is the metal ion drawn in a dot and cross diagram of sodium chloride?
misconceptions.correct: With its outer shell empty, in square brackets, with the charge written outside the brackets.
misconceptions.misconception: You still draw sodium's outer electron, because sodium still has that electron somewhere in the diagram.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students draw the two atoms first and then add an arrow, leaving the original electron in place rather than redrawing the shells after transfer.
misconceptions.correction: The diagram must show the situation after transfer. Sodium's outer shell is now empty, drawn as [Na]+ with 2,8 remaining, and the transferred electron appears in the chlorine as one of the eight, drawn as [Cl]- with the transferred electron marked as a cross.

misconceptions.question: How many chloride ions are needed for one magnesium ion?
misconceptions.correct: Two, because Mg2+ needs two Cl- ions to balance the charge, giving MgCl2.
misconceptions.misconception: Magnesium is 2+ and chlorine is 1-, so one of each pairs up to make MgCl.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The one-to-one picture of sodium chloride is learned first and applied to every ionic compound without checking that the charges balance.
misconceptions.correction: Balance the charges to zero. One Mg2+ contributes 2+, so two Cl- ions are needed to contribute 2-. Magnesium has two outer electrons and each chlorine atom can accept only one, so two chlorine atoms are required.

misconceptions.question: Is there such a thing as a molecule of sodium chloride?
misconceptions.correct: No. An ionic compound is a giant structure of ions, and the electrostatic forces act in all directions in the lattice.
misconceptions.misconception: The formula NaCl means one sodium ion is bonded to its own chloride partner, so the solid is made of NaCl molecules.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The formula looks exactly like a molecular formula, and dot and cross diagrams show a single pair of ions, which reinforces the idea of a pair that belongs together.
misconceptions.correction: NaCl is an empirical formula - it gives the ratio, not a molecule. In the lattice each ion is surrounded by ions of opposite charge and attracts all of them, in all directions, so no single partner can be picked out.

misconceptions.question: A model shows 14 sodium ions and 13 chloride ions. What is the formula?
misconceptions.correct: NaCl - the empirical formula is the simplest whole number ratio, and the model shows a ratio of about 1:1.
misconceptions.misconception: You write down exactly what you counted, so the formula is Na14Cl13.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students transfer the counting method used for molecular formulae, where the actual number of atoms is what is wanted, to a giant structure where only the ratio has meaning.
misconceptions.correction: A model of a giant structure shows only a fragment, and ions at the edges are cut off, which is why the counts are not exactly equal. Reduce the counts to the simplest whole number ratio: 1 sodium to 1 chloride, so NaCl.

misconceptions.question: What is wrong with a ball and stick model?
misconceptions.correct: The sticks are not real, and the model shows the particles much further apart than they really are.
misconceptions.misconception: Ball and stick models are accurate pictures - the gaps between the balls show the real empty space inside the substance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The model is solid, three-dimensional and used in class as though it were the thing itself, so students read it literally rather than as a deliberate simplification.
misconceptions.correction: State the limitation precisely: bonds are forces, not rods, and in the real structure the particles touch. The model also shows only a tiny part of what is a giant structure.

misconceptions.question: Are the covalent bonds in a small molecule weak?
misconceptions.correct: No. The covalent bonds between atoms in a molecule are strong.
misconceptions.misconception: Substances like water and methane melt and boil easily, so the covalent bonds holding them together must be weak.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students have one mental slot for 'the forces in this substance' and fill it from the melting point, without separating the bonds inside a molecule from the forces between molecules.
misconceptions.correction: Distinguish the two. The covalent bonds within the molecule are strong - the specification says so directly. What is easily overcome when a molecular substance melts is the attraction between separate molecules, not the bonds inside them.

misconceptions.question: Is a polymer a giant covalent structure?
misconceptions.correct: No. Some covalently bonded substances have very large molecules, such as polymers - the polymer is a molecule, not a lattice.
misconceptions.misconception: A polymer contains thousands of atoms, so it must be giant covalent like diamond.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Very large' and 'giant' sound like the same idea, and both types have many atoms held by strong covalent bonds.
misconceptions.correction: The specification lists them separately. A polymer is a long chain molecule with a definite start and end; a giant covalent structure such as diamond or silicon dioxide is bonded in every direction with no separate molecules at all.

misconceptions.question: Is silicon dioxide made of SiO2 molecules?
misconceptions.correct: No. Silicon dioxide has a giant covalent structure, and SiO2 is its empirical formula.
misconceptions.misconception: SiO2 looks just like CO2, so silicon dioxide must be made of small molecules in the same way.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two formulae are written identically, and students take the formula as evidence of a molecule without asking whether the substance is molecular or giant.
misconceptions.correction: Learn the specification's examples: diamond and silicon dioxide are the named giant covalent structures. In silicon dioxide every silicon atom is covalently bonded to oxygen atoms throughout the structure, so SiO2 gives the ratio, not a molecule.

misconceptions.question: Is every covalent bond a single shared pair?
misconceptions.correct: No. Oxygen has two shared pairs between the atoms and nitrogen has three.
misconceptions.misconception: A covalent bond means one shared pair, so O2 and N2 each have one pair shared between the two atoms.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The first molecules met are H2, HCl, H2O and CH4, all of which have only single bonds, so students generalise from that set.
misconceptions.correction: Count what each atom needs. Oxygen is 2,6 and needs two more electrons, so two pairs are shared - a double bond. Nitrogen is 2,5 and needs three, so three pairs are shared - a triple bond. Each atom then has eight outer electrons.

misconceptions.question: What does one line in a displayed formula stand for?
misconceptions.correct: One shared pair of electrons, that is one single covalent bond.
misconceptions.misconception: The line is one electron, so a molecule with four lines has four electrons in its bonds.
misconceptions.whyItArises: One line looks like one thing, and the link back to the dot and cross diagram, where each bond is drawn as two electrons, is not made explicit.
misconceptions.correction: Convert between the two representations. Every line in a displayed formula replaces one shared pair, so methane's four lines stand for eight bonding electrons, and a double bond is drawn as two lines.

misconceptions.question: What does the n mean in the formula of a polymer?
misconceptions.correct: It shows that the repeating unit inside the brackets is repeated a large number of times.
misconceptions.misconception: The n is a number you have to work out, like the number of carbon atoms or the number of monomers used.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every other subscript in chemistry is a definite number, so a letter in the same position is read as an unknown waiting to be found.
misconceptions.correction: The specification simply states that n is a large number. It is not a fixed value and different molecules of the same polymer have different values of n, which is why the letter is used.

misconceptions.question: Do delocalised electrons still belong to particular metal atoms?
misconceptions.correct: No. The electrons in the outer shell of metal atoms are delocalised and so are free to move through the whole structure.
misconceptions.misconception: Each metal atom keeps its own outer electrons but holds them loosely, so they wobble a bit within their own shell.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every earlier model of the atom fixes electrons in shells around one nucleus, and 'delocalised' is a new word that is easy to say without changing that picture.
misconceptions.correction: Delocalised means no longer associated with any one atom. The outer electrons form a sea spread through the whole giant structure, and it is the sharing of these delocalised electrons that gives rise to strong metallic bonds.

misconceptions.question: Is a metal held together by attraction between positive and negative ions?
misconceptions.correct: No. Metals consist of giant structures of atoms, and the strong metallic bonds come from the sharing of delocalised electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: The diagram of a metal shows plus signs and loose electrons, so metallic bonding is really ionic bonding with electrons as the negative ions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The standard representation marks the metal particles with a positive charge, and students match that against the picture of an ionic lattice they already know.
misconceptions.correction: Ionic bonding requires two kinds of ion, formed by transferring electrons from one substance to another. In a metal nothing is transferred away - the outer electrons are shared by all the atoms at once, which is what the plus signs and the sea of electrons are drawn to show.

misconceptions.question: How do you read a molecular formula off a ball and stick model?
misconceptions.correct: Count the balls of each colour - the atoms - and ignore the sticks, which are the bonds.
misconceptions.misconception: Every stick joins something on, so the sticks should be counted in as well when working out the formula.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students count everything visible in the model rather than deciding first which parts represent atoms and which represent bonds.
misconceptions.correction: Identify the elements from the key, then count only the balls. A model with one black ball and four white balls is CH4 - the four sticks are the four covalent bonds, not extra atoms.

misconceptions.question: Does the formula NaCl mean sodium chloride is a small molecule?
misconceptions.correct: No. Sodium chloride is ionic and NaCl is the ratio of ions in a giant structure.
misconceptions.misconception: A short formula with two symbols in it means a small molecule, so NaCl is a molecule just like HCl.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students judge from the appearance of the formula alone, because HCl, CO2 and NaCl all look alike written down.
misconceptions.correction: Look at the elements, not the length of the formula. Sodium is a metal, so NaCl is ionic; hydrogen and chlorine are both non-metals, so HCl is a small molecule. Small molecules are made only of non-metals.

misconceptions.question: Does a covalent bond act in all directions like an ionic bond?
misconceptions.correct: No. In an ionic lattice the electrostatic forces act in all directions; a covalent bond is a shared pair between two particular atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: All strong bonds work the same way, so the atoms in a molecule attract every other atom around them equally.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The phrase 'act in all directions' is memorised as a general fact about bonding rather than as the specific feature of an ionic lattice that the specification states.
misconceptions.correction: Keep the phrase where it belongs. It describes ionic bonding in the lattice. A covalent bond involves a shared pair of electrons between two named atoms, which is why molecules have definite shapes and definite formulae.

misconceptions.question: Is a shared pair one electron or two?
misconceptions.correct: A shared pair is two electrons, one contributed by each atom, and it forms one covalent bond.
misconceptions.misconception: Each atom puts in an electron and that electron is the bond, so counting the shared electrons gives the number of bonds.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students count the dots and crosses in the overlap region individually, because the diagram shows separate marks rather than an obvious pair.
misconceptions.correction: Count pairs, not marks. In the overlap of a single bond there is one dot and one cross - two electrons making one bond. Oxygen shows four electrons in the overlap, which is two pairs, so a double bond.

misconceptions.question: Should a molecular formula be simplified to its lowest ratio?
misconceptions.correct: No. A molecular formula gives the actual number of atoms of each element in the molecule.
misconceptions.misconception: Formulae should always be written in the simplest form, so a model of ethene, C2H4, should be written as CH2.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Empirical formulae are practised for ionic compounds just before this, and students carry the habit of simplifying across to molecules.
misconceptions.correction: Match the method to the question. For a giant ionic structure work out the simplest ratio; for a molecule count the atoms and leave the numbers alone. C2H4 is the molecular formula of ethene and must not be reduced.

mcqs.stem: In metallic bonding, the specification describes the particles as:

options.text: atoms that share delocalised electrons
options.rationale: This is the specification's wording: for metallic bonding the particles are atoms which share delocalised electrons.

options.text: positive ions attracted to negative ions
options.rationale: The usual diagram of a metal marks the particles with plus signs, so students read it as an ionic lattice.

options.text: atoms that each keep their own outer electrons
options.rationale: Students keep the shell picture and miss what delocalised means.

options.text: atoms that share a single pair of electrons
options.rationale: This is the definition of covalent bonding, chosen when the three bond types are not kept apart.

mcqs.stem: Magnesium oxide is formed from magnesium and oxygen. What bonding does it contain?

options.text: Covalent, because two different elements have combined
options.rationale: Students who treat all compounds alike pick a bond type without checking for a metal.

options.text: Ionic, because a metal has combined with a non-metal
options.rationale: Magnesium is a metal and oxygen a non-metal, and ionic bonding occurs in compounds formed from metals combined with non-metals.

options.text: Metallic, because one of the elements is a metal
options.rationale: Metallic bonding is assumed whenever a metal appears, ignoring that this is a compound with a non-metal.

options.text: Covalent, because oxygen needs two more electrons
options.rationale: The electron requirement of oxygen is correct but it is met by transfer here, not by sharing.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about covalent bonding is correct?

options.text: It occurs only in compounds, and never in elements such as oxygen
options.rationale: Students link bonding to compounds only, so O2 is not seen as bonded.

options.text: It occurs whenever two atoms of different elements join together
options.rationale: Attractive to students who classify by 'different elements' rather than by metal or non-metal.

options.text: It occurs in most non-metallic elements and in compounds of non-metals
options.rationale: This is the specification statement for where covalent bonding is found.

options.text: It occurs in non-metal elements but not in compounds of non-metals
options.rationale: The reverse over-correction, restricting covalent bonding to elements alone.

mcqs.stem: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. The bonding in brass is:

options.text: ionic, because copper and zinc are different elements
options.rationale: Students treat any two elements together as a compound and reach for ionic bonding.

options.text: covalent, because the two metals share outer electrons
options.rationale: The word 'share' appears in both covalent and metallic bonding, and students pick the more familiar one.

options.text: metallic in the copper but absent in the zinc
options.rationale: Assumes bonding belongs to one element rather than to the whole structure.

options.text: metallic, because metallic bonding occurs in alloys
options.rationale: The specification states that metallic bonding occurs in metallic elements and alloys.

mcqs.stem: Why is the ionic bond in sodium chloride described as strong?

options.text: There are strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions
options.rationale: Chemical bonding is explained in terms of electrostatic forces, and the ionic bond is the attraction between the ions formed.

options.text: The transfer of the electron from sodium to chlorine is itself the bond
options.rationale: The transfer is the memorable step, so students name it as the bond.

options.text: Pairs of electrons are shared strongly by the sodium and the chlorine
options.rationale: Sharing is imported from covalent bonding into an ionic compound.

options.text: The ions are packed so tightly that they cannot physically move apart
options.rationale: Close packing is a consequence of the attraction, not the reason for the bond's strength.

mcqs.stem: A sodium atom (2,8,1) reacts with a chlorine atom (2,8,7). What happens to the electrons?

options.text: Sodium gains seven electrons to complete its outer shell
options.rationale: Students apply 'fill the outer shell' without asking which atom is the metal.

options.text: Sodium loses one electron and chlorine gains one electron
options.rationale: Electrons in the outer shell of the metal atom are transferred; the metal loses and the non-metal gains.

options.text: Sodium gains one electron and so becomes positively charged
options.rationale: Gain and positive are wrongly paired by students who do not track the charge balance.

options.text: Sodium and chlorine share one pair of electrons between them
options.rationale: Sharing describes covalent bonding, not a metal reacting with a non-metal.

mcqs.stem: An oxygen atom has the electronic structure 2,6. What is the electronic structure of the oxide ion?

options.rationale: Students assume the ion keeps the atom's electron arrangement because it is still oxygen.
Chosen by students who reach for argon because they think every ion must have eight outer electrons in a third shell.
Oxygen is in Group 6, so it gains two electrons; 2,6 becomes 2,8, the electronic structure of neon.
Assumes oxygen loses electrons rather than gains them.

mcqs.stem: An element in Group 2 of the periodic table forms an ion. What is the charge on that ion?

options.rationale: The number is right but the sign is reversed by students who link losing to negative.
Comes from counting the six electrons needed to fill the shell instead of the two that are lost.
Taken from the eight electrons in a full outer shell rather than from the group number.
Group 2 metals lose their two outer electrons, so the charge is 2+ and matches the group number.

mcqs.stem: Potassium is in Group 1 and sulfur is in Group 6. Which pair of ion charges is correct?

options.text: K+ and S2-
options.rationale: Group 1 metals lose one electron to form 1+ ions; Group 6 non-metals gain two to form 2- ions.

options.text: K+ and S6-
options.rationale: The charge is taken straight from the group number for the non-metal as well as the metal.

options.text: K- and S2+
options.rationale: Both signs are reversed by a student who has lose and gain the wrong way round.

options.text: K2+ and S2-
options.rationale: The metal charge is matched to the non-metal charge instead of being read from Group 1.

mcqs.stem: In a dot and cross diagram for sodium chloride, the sodium ion should be drawn showing:

options.text: one outer electron, in square brackets with a + charge
options.rationale: Students add the charge but forget to remove the electron they have already transferred.

options.text: an empty outer shell, in square brackets with a + charge
options.rationale: After transfer sodium has 2,8, so no outer electrons are drawn, and the ion is shown in brackets with its charge.

options.text: one outer electron, with no brackets and no charge shown
options.rationale: The atom is drawn unchanged because the ion is thought to keep the atom's structure.

options.text: eight outer electrons, in square brackets with a - charge
options.rationale: This is the chloride ion, chosen when the two ions are confused.

mcqs.stem: A dot and cross diagram is drawn for magnesium chloride. What should it show?

options.text: One chloride ion, with a charge of 2-
options.rationale: Students pair the ions one to one and put the balancing charge on the single chloride.

options.text: Two chloride ions, each with a charge of 7-
options.rationale: The number of ions is right but the charge is read off the group number.

options.text: Two chloride ions, each with a charge of 1-
options.rationale: Magnesium loses two electrons, one to each chlorine atom, giving Mg2+ and two Cl- ions.

options.text: One chloride ion, with a charge of 1-
options.rationale: Copies the one-to-one pattern of sodium chloride and leaves the charges unbalanced.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes the bonding in a giant ionic lattice?

options.text: Each positive ion is bonded to one negative ion beside it
options.rationale: The formula and dot and cross diagram suggest a partner ion, so students imagine molecules.

options.text: Electrons transfer continuously between the ions in the lattice
options.rationale: Transfer is treated as the ongoing bond rather than as the step that made the ions.

options.text: Weak forces act between ions that are themselves very strong
options.rationale: Confuses the strength of the forces with the properties of the particles.

options.text: Strong electrostatic forces act in all directions between the ions
options.rationale: The specification states that these forces act in all directions in the lattice, and this is called ionic bonding.

mcqs.stem: A diagram shows a regular repeating array of alternating Na+ and Cl- particles. What can be deduced?

options.text: It is ionic, because oppositely charged ions are arranged in a lattice
options.rationale: Charged particles arranged in a repeating lattice is the diagnostic feature of an ionic compound.

options.text: It is molecular, because each sodium is paired with one chlorine
options.rationale: Students see the 1:1 ratio and read it as a molecule rather than as a ratio.

options.text: It is covalent, because sodium and chlorine share electrons here
options.rationale: Sharing is assumed to underlie all bonding, so the charges are overlooked.

options.text: It is metallic, because the particles form a regular pattern
options.rationale: A regular pattern alone is used as the test, ignoring that the particles are charged ions.

mcqs.stem: What is a limitation of a two-dimensional diagram of the sodium chloride lattice?

options.text: It shows the ions touching when they are really far apart
options.rationale: The spacing criticism belongs to ball and stick models, and is stated the wrong way round here.

options.text: It cannot show that the lattice extends in three dimensions
options.rationale: A flat diagram loses the third dimension, so the forces acting in all directions cannot be shown.

options.text: It shows the wrong ratio of sodium ions to chloride ions
options.rationale: A correctly drawn diagram shows the 1:1 ratio, so this is not a limitation of the model.

options.text: It shows ions rather than the molecules that are present
options.rationale: Chosen by students who believe sodium chloride is made of molecules.

mcqs.stem: What is a limitation of using a ball and stick model for a giant structure?

options.text: It shows the particles at correct spacing but only in two dimensions
options.rationale: Students who read the model literally think the spacing is accurate.

options.text: It cannot show the ratio in which the particles are joined
options.rationale: The ratio is one of the few things the model does show clearly.

options.text: It shows the particles too far apart and bonds as solid sticks
options.rationale: Bonds are forces, not rods, and the model exaggerates the space between the particles.

options.text: It shows a giant structure as though it were one small molecule
options.rationale: Attractive to students who already treat giant structures as molecular.

mcqs.stem: A model of an ionic compound shows 4 calcium ions and 8 fluoride ions. Its empirical formula is:

options.text: Ca4F8
options.rationale: The counted numbers are written down without being simplified.

options.text: Ca2F
options.rationale: The ratio is simplified but written the wrong way round.

options.text: CaF
options.rationale: Assumes ionic compounds always pair one ion with one ion.

options.text: CaF2
options.rationale: The ratio 4:8 simplifies to 1:2, and the empirical formula is the simplest whole number ratio of the ions.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the covalent bonds inside a water molecule is correct?

options.text: They are strong bonds between the atoms in the molecule
options.rationale: The specification states directly that the covalent bonds between atoms are strong.

options.text: They are weak, because water boils at quite a low temperature
options.rationale: Students judge bond strength from the melting or boiling point of the substance.

options.text: They are formed by electrons transferring between the atoms
options.rationale: Transfer is imported from ionic bonding into a covalent molecule.

options.text: They are strong only where two pairs of electrons are shared
options.rationale: Assumes single bonds are weak and only multiple bonds count as strong.

mcqs.stem: Which formula represents a substance that consists of small molecules?

options.text: NaCl
options.rationale: The short formula looks molecular, but sodium is a metal so this is a giant ionic structure.

options.text: CO2
options.rationale: Carbon and oxygen are both non-metals and carbon dioxide consists of small molecules.

options.text: SiO2
options.rationale: Written like CO2, but silicon dioxide is a named giant covalent structure.

options.text: Cu
options.rationale: Copper is a metallic element with a giant structure of atoms, not a molecule.

mcqs.stem: Poly(ethene) and diamond are both covalently bonded. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Both are giant covalent structures because both have many atoms
options.rationale: 'Very large' and 'giant' are treated as the same category.

options.text: Both consist of small molecules held by weak covalent bonds
options.rationale: Combines the idea that all covalent substances are molecular with weak bonds.

options.text: Poly(ethene) has very large molecules; diamond is giant covalent
options.rationale: The specification lists polymers as very large molecules and diamond as a giant covalent structure.

options.text: Poly(ethene) is giant covalent; diamond has large molecules
options.rationale: The two categories are correctly named but applied to the wrong substances.

mcqs.stem: A polymer is drawn as a repeating unit inside brackets with a subscript n. The n shows that:

options.text: the polymer molecule contains exactly n carbon atoms in total
options.rationale: Students read n as a subscript giving a count of atoms.

options.text: the structure inside the brackets is a giant covalent lattice
options.rationale: Attractive to students who classify polymers as giant covalent.

options.text: n pairs of electrons are shared inside the repeating unit
options.rationale: The subscript is read as a count of bonding electrons instead of repeats.

options.text: the unit in the brackets is repeated a large number of times
options.rationale: The specification states that n is a large number, describing how many times the repeating unit occurs.

mcqs.stem: How many pairs of electrons are shared between the two atoms in an oxygen molecule, O2?

options.text: Two
options.rationale: Each oxygen atom (2,6) needs two more electrons, so two pairs are shared, giving each atom eight outer electrons.

options.text: One
options.rationale: Every covalent bond is assumed to be a single shared pair.

options.text: Four
options.rationale: The four shared electrons are counted individually instead of as two pairs.

options.text: Three
options.rationale: This is the number of shared pairs in nitrogen, N2, and the two molecules are confused.

mcqs.stem: In a dot and cross diagram of ammonia, NH3, the nitrogen atom is shown with:

options.text: three shared electrons and five that are not shared
options.rationale: Individual electrons are counted rather than shared pairs.

options.text: three shared pairs and one pair that is not shared
options.rationale: Nitrogen is 2,5; three electrons are shared with hydrogen atoms and the remaining two form a non-bonding pair, giving eight outer electrons.

options.text: three shared pairs and no other outer shell electrons
options.rationale: Students draw only the bonds and forget nitrogen's fifth outer electron.

options.text: four shared pairs, with one spare pair to each hydrogen
options.rationale: Assumes nitrogen forms four bonds like carbon in methane.

mcqs.stem: In a displayed formula, what does one line drawn between two atoms represent?

options.text: One single electron passed from one atom to the other atom
options.rationale: The line is counted as one electron because it looks like one thing.

options.text: The transfer of an electron from one atom to another atom
options.rationale: Transfer is imported from ionic bonding into a covalent representation.

options.text: One shared pair of electrons, that is a single covalent bond
options.rationale: The specification uses a line to represent a single bond, which is one shared pair of electrons.

options.text: Two shared pairs of electrons held between the two atoms
options.rationale: Confuses a single line with a double bond, which is drawn as two lines.

mcqs.stem: A ball and stick model shows one black ball joined by four sticks to four white balls. Black is carbon and white is hydrogen. The molecular formula is:

options.text: C4H4
options.rationale: The four sticks are counted as extra carbon atoms.

options.text: CH
options.rationale: The formula is simplified to a ratio, which is wrong for a molecular formula.

options.text: C4H
options.rationale: The atom counts are attached to the wrong elements.

options.text: CH4
options.rationale: One carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms; the sticks are the four covalent bonds, not atoms.

mcqs.stem: Why are the outer electrons in a metal able to move through the whole structure?

options.text: They are delocalised, so they are not held by any one atom
options.rationale: The specification states that outer shell electrons are delocalised and so are free to move through the whole structure.

options.text: They are held loosely in the outer shell of their own atom
options.rationale: The shell picture is kept and 'delocalised' is read as 'loosely held'.

options.text: They are attracted to the negative ions within the lattice
options.rationale: The metal is pictured as an ionic lattice with two kinds of ion.

options.text: They are shared in pairs between neighbouring metal atoms
options.rationale: Describes covalent bonding rather than the shared sea of delocalised electrons.

mcqs.stem: Which phrase describes the structure of a pure metal?

options.text: A giant structure of atoms joined by shared pairs of electrons
options.rationale: 'Giant structure' is correct but the sharing is described as covalent.

options.text: A giant structure of atoms arranged in a regular pattern
options.rationale: This is the specification's description of the structure of a metal.

options.text: A lattice of positive and negative ions attracting each other
options.rationale: The positive charges in the usual diagram are read as an ionic lattice.

options.text: Small molecules of metal atoms packed closely together
options.rationale: Applies the molecular picture to a substance that has a giant structure.
